passage: In Himani's village near Mandi, the only chemist folded every leaflet into the box, and Himani read hers twice by the kitchen lamp. Headache. Dizziness. Dry mouth. Tingling hands. Upset stomach. By bedtime she had noticed all five. Her mouth felt like paper, her fingers prickled, and a small ache sat behind her eyes. "I have everything on the list," she whispered to her cousin Pallavi, who was folding clothes. Pallavi looked up. "You took the first tablet after dinner. You also ran up the hill in the sun today and drank no water." Himani laughed shakily and filled a steel tumbler. The prickling faded. "But if the headache stays," Pallavi added, "you tell the doctor at the clinic. Not me, not the leaflet."

qa.q: How many of the listed effects had Himani noticed by bedtime?
qa.a: All five.

qa.q: Why did Himani notice every listed effect so quickly?
qa.a: Having just read the list twice, she was scanning her body with fear, so ordinary feelings like a dry mouth after the sun felt like side effects. 😰

qa.q: What sensible plan did Pallavi add at the end?
qa.a: If the headache stays, Himani should tell the doctor at the clinic rather than rely on a cousin or the leaflet; fear can magnify twinges, but a lasting symptom still needs a doctor.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see Himani's worry?
qa.a: Pallavi sees ordinary reasons, running in the sun and no water, and points them out gently, taking Himani seriously while trying to calm the fear.

grounding: A young woman reading a medicine leaflet starts feeling every listed effect, while her cousin reminds her a lasting symptom still needs the doctor.

passage: Pablo's flat in Valencia was quiet except for the fridge. He had spread the leaflet from his new hay fever tablets across the whole table: three columns of tiny print. "Common: drowsiness, headache, stomach upset. Rare: heart flutter." Soon he had pressed two fingers to his wrist four times. Was that a flutter? His stomach did feel strange. His head felt heavy. When Jamal came in with shopping bags, Pablo said, "I think I'm having a reaction." Jamal looked at the leaflet, then at him. "You've been reading that thing for an hour, mate. Anyone would feel ill reading about it for an hour." Pablo gave a tight laugh. He folded the paper away, but wrote down how he felt, to tell the doctor if it kept going.

qa.q: What was listed as a rare effect on the leaflet?
qa.a: Heart flutter.

qa.q: Why did Pablo keep pressing his fingers to his wrist?
qa.a: He was afraid of the rare heart flutter he had just read about, so he kept checking, and every small sensation seemed like a sign of it.

qa.q: What choice did Pablo make at the end that balances fear and care?
qa.a: He put the leaflet away to stop feeding the worry, but wrote down how he felt so he could tell the doctor if it kept going.

qa.q: How might Jamal see the scene on walking in?
qa.a: Jamal sees a friend who has spent an hour over tiny print; to Jamal the reading itself looks like part of the problem, so the reply is gentle teasing rather than alarm.

grounding: A young man reading a long medicine leaflet begins to feel each listed effect, then sets it aside while still planning to tell the doctor if symptoms persist.

passage: In the campus clinic waiting room, Gopika had nothing to do but read the leaflet from her new skin cream. By the third paragraph, her cheeks felt hot. By the fifth, she was sure her lips were tingling. She kept touching her face and checking it in her phone camera. "Gopika?" Arnab, the nursing intern at the desk, called her name. She hurried up. "I think I'm reacting. It says burning, tingling, redness." Arnab looked at her skin carefully. "I don't see redness. Did the feeling start before or after you read it?" Gopika paused. "After." "Worry can turn up the volume on sensations," he said kindly. "Tell the doctor exactly what you felt. If it keeps happening, they'll want to know."

qa.q: Where was Gopika when she read the leaflet?
qa.a: In the campus clinic waiting room.

qa.q: What does Gopika checking her face in the phone camera suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was growing anxious that the cream was harming her, and the worry made her watch for, and feel, the effects she had just read about.

qa.q: Which question from Arnab helped Gopika, and why?
qa.a: "Did the feeling start before or after you read it?" It helped her notice that fear might be adding to the sensations, while he still told her to report it to the doctor.

qa.q: How does Arnab see the situation compared with Gopika?
qa.a: Arnab looks calmly and sees no redness, so he treats the worry kindly rather than as an emergency, while Gopika is sure she is reacting.

grounding: A student reading a cream's leaflet in a clinic begins to feel the listed effects, and a nursing intern helps her notice the role of fear while still involving the doctor.

passage:
Subject: I read the whole leaflet (mistake)

Salma,
You know how the college doctor gave me the new allergy tablets? I took the first one last night and then, like an idiot, unfolded the leaflet. It's a metre long. Drowsiness, dry mouth, headache, blurred vision, itching, racing heart.
By midnight I had all of them. My mouth was dry, my eyes felt funny, and I kept checking my pulse. I didn't sleep till three.
This morning at practical, I forgot to worry for two hours and felt completely normal. So I think most of it was me reading.
But one thing is real: there's an itchy red patch on my arm that's still there, and it's getting bigger. I'm not going to talk myself out of that. Booked the college clinic for tomorrow.
Come for chai after? I need someone to laugh at me.
Kiran

qa.q: What did the college doctor give Kiran?
qa.a: The college doctor gave Kiran the new allergy tablets.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling after reading the leaflet at night?
qa.a: Kiran was frightened and on edge, checking the pulse and unable to sleep till three because every listed effect seemed to be happening.

qa.q: What did Kiran decide about the red patch, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Kiran booked the college clinic, because a patch that stays and grows is real and deserves a doctor's attention even if the other twinges came from worry.

qa.q: How might Salma feel reading this email?
qa.a: Salma would likely feel amused by the 'metre long' leaflet but also glad Kiran is getting the red patch checked.

grounding: A young adult who reads a long side-effect leaflet feels every twinge, sees that fear magnified most of it, and still takes a persistent symptom to the doctor.

passage: Vishal, sit, you have to hear this. I'm Rajni, sensible Rajni, the girl who reads instructions, right? Last Tuesday the dentist gave me a mouthwash for my gums. Fine. Then at one in the morning I read the leaflet by phone light. Tingling tongue. Changed taste. Burning. Rare: swelling of the face. So I lay there poking my tongue against my teeth. Tingly? Maybe tingly. I got up and checked my face in the bathroom mirror four times. My roommate Leena woke up and said, 'Rajni, your face is exactly your face.' In the morning I went to the chemist downstairs, and the pharmacist read the leaflet with me, slowly. She said most people get none of it, and that if anything keeps going or worries me, I should go back to the dentist. By lunch I'd forgotten all about my tongue. Honestly, the scariest thing was the leaflet at one a.m.

qa.q: What did Leena say on waking up?
qa.a: Leena said, 'Rajni, your face is exactly your face.'

qa.q: Why did Rajni check her face in the mirror four times?
qa.a: After reading about rare swelling in the middle of the night, she was scared, and the fear made every small feeling seem like a symptom.

qa.q: Which step helped Rajni most, and why?
qa.a: Going over the leaflet slowly with the pharmacist gave her balanced information and a clear plan to return to the dentist if anything kept going.

qa.q: How might Leena have felt being woken up at one in the morning?
qa.a: Leena was probably sleepy and a little amused, but Leena's joke also helped calm Rajni.

grounding: A young woman reading a leaflet at night feels each listed effect out of fear, then gets balanced information and knows to return to the dentist if anything persists.
